title: The Year Merrill Fernando Finally Put Dilmah on the Packet
dek: After three decades selling Ceylon tea in bulk for others to blend and brand, a Colombo trader launched his own label in 1988.

story.event: Launching his own single-origin tea brand after decades of selling tea in bulk
story.summary: As a young trainee in London's tea trade in the 1950s, Merrill J. Fernando saw Ceylon tea blended with cheaper teas and branded abroad, and resolved to have his own brand. He spent three decades exporting bulk tea and packing tea under other labels, registered the name Dilmah in 1974, and in 1988 launched it as an unblended, Sri Lankan-packed brand, first on Coles shelves in Australia. Dilmah grew into one of the world's larger tea brands; he died in 2023.
paragraphs: In the mid-1950s Merrill J. Fernando, a trainee tea taster from Ceylon in his twenties, was sent to Mincing Lane in London, then the centre of the world's tea trade. He was disappointed by what he found there. Ceylon tea, he later recalled, was mixed with cruder teas from elsewhere and still labelled Ceylon, and the island was paid for its leaf as a raw material while the money from blending, packing and branding was made abroad. "The thought of having my own brand haunted me," he told the writer Jack Yan in 2014.

For more than thirty years he did not act on it. He founded Merrill J. Fernando & Co. in 1962 to export bulk tea, sold it in the 1970s after nationalisation and new controls made him lose heart, then started again with MJF Exports. In 1974 he registered a brand name made from his sons' names, Dilhan and Malik, and left it unused. Through the 1980s he packed tea under other companies' labels for Australian retailers including Coles, Woolworths and Franklins, learning the market from the inside, while bulk sales to the Soviet Union paid well.

In 1988 he decided to put Dilmah on the packet. Some of his buyers told him he would never succeed because he was too far from the customer. "I started with very little money," he said later. "I realized if it failed, I would have lost all the money I had made." Earlier reports, by the journalist Eric Ellis in 2007 and Sri Lanka's Sunday Times in 2013, say his Soviet earnings paid for the launch. According to the trade magazine STIR, Coles agreed to stock two Dilmah teas, sold as premium unblended tea packed in Sri Lanka. Australia was the market he knew best; he had sold bulk tea there since the 1960s.

The brand reached New Zealand and, through the 1990s, Europe and North America. When counterfeit packs appeared, he printed the brand's story on the box, and later his photograph. Australians came to know his face from television advertisements ending with his words "do try it". In 2009 Euromonitor counted Dilmah among the world's eight largest tea brands. Fernando died in Colombo in July 2023, aged 93.

quote.text: There is no single recipe for making the perfect tea, as there are no rules for producing a Titian or a Sesson. Each preparation of the leaves has its individuality, its special affinity with water and heat, its own method of telling a story.
quote.source_title: The Book of Tea, Project Gutenberg eBook #769
quote.connection: Okakura would have agreed with Fernando that each tea has its own story to tell, and that blending can bury it. He would also have doubted that any one way of making tea is the only honest one. Fernando built a brand on that certainty; Okakura leaves the question open.

reflection: Fernando carried his idea for more than thirty years before he acted on it. In the meantime he did ordinary work: tasting, shipping, packing other people's brands, learning how Australian shoppers chose a packet from a shelf. When he finally moved he knew the market from the inside, and he still called it a risk.

Some of your plans may be waiting in a similar way. Waiting is not always avoidance; sometimes it is the years in which you learn what the plan will need. The question worth asking now and then is whether you are still learning, or only waiting.
invitation: Take one idea you have carried for a long time. Write down one thing you have learned since you first had it that makes it more possible now, and leave it there for today.

sources.title: Philanthropist and Dilmah Tea founder Merrill J. Fernando passes away at 93

Fernando & Co. founded in 1962; selling the business amid nationalisation and regulation; MJF Exports; 1980s own-label supply to Coles, Tetley, Woolworths and Franklins in Australia; the 1988 launch at substantial risk, with buyers saying he was not close enough to the customer; 'I started with very little money' and 'I realized if it failed, I would have lost all the money I had made'.

sources.title: Founder of Dilmah tea leaves a storied legacy
sources.supports: Sent to London's Mincing Lane for training in 1956; decades as a taster, trader and bulk seller; private-label packing for major retailers; in 1988 Coles accepted two Dilmah teas priced as premium unblended leaf packed at origin; described as the first marketer of a branded single country-of-origin tea.

cross_checks.claim: In London's Mincing Lane in the 1950s Fernando saw Ceylon tea blended with other teas and resolved to have his own brand.
He registered the Dilmah name in 1974 and did not launch it until 1988.
Before 1988 he packed tea under other labels for Australian retailers such as Coles.
Dilmah was launched as a brand in Australia in 1988.
Soviet bulk-tea earnings helped pay for the launch.

research_notes: Dates of his London training differ: the Sunday Times (2013) has him training as a taster from 1950 and dating his 'own brand' vision to 1954; WIPO says he went to Mincing Lane at 24 (about 1954) for two years; STIR says 1956; Lucire says he applied in 1952 and was in the first batch sent to London. The story says 'the mid-1950s'. Money: in 2014 he told Jack Yan he 'started with very little money' and stood to lose all he had made; Eric Ellis (2007) reports a Soviet-era windfall ('more money than I knew what do with' in Ellis's text) that helped set up Dilmah, and the Sunday Times (2013) says the Russian trade provided the investment for the Australian launch. The story gives his 2014 words and notes the earlier accounts beside them. Ellis also says his Soviet and Eastern European bulk markets were collapsing by 1988; the story leaves that out because the Sunday Times describes the Russian trade as still lucrative. First Coles business: WIPO describes a mid-1980s deal under Coles's own label, tested at one store and then nationwide, before the independent launch in 1988; STIR says Coles accepted two Dilmah-branded teas in 1988. The story uses both in sequence. The founding year is sometimes given as 1985 (CNA, not cited) or 1974 (the trademark); the brand launch is dated 1988 by WIPO, STIR, Ellis, the Sunday Times, AAP and Newstalk ZB. The 'do try it' line: AAP says Australians knew it from a television advertisement; Newstalk ZB (not cited) says the same of New Zealand. Lucire's obituary is by its publisher Jack Yan, who interviewed Fernando and wrote about Dilmah in a book; the 2014 quotations are his. The company field adds MJF Group to distinguish the brand from the bulk-trading firms. Okakura is writing about the art of preparing tea, not blending for trade; the quote is applied by analogy.
